newsitem.title: ITALY: Mini-budget won't loosen Bank of Italy's iron grip.
newsitem.headline: Mini-budget won't loosen Bank of Italy's iron grip.

text.p: A stopgap mini-budget, the weak lira and concerns that Europe's single currency may be delayed will prevent the Bank of Italy from lowering interest rates for the foreseeable future, economists said on Thursday.
They believe Italy's latest 15.5 trillion lire ($9.2 billion) package to plug widening gaps in its budget deficit is a short-term measure which does little to help market confidence.

"In these circumstances I don't think the Bank of Italy will ease monetary policy," said Pio de Gregorio, economist at NatWest Markets here. "The Bank of Italy governor remains worried we could have another spell of weakness on the lira."

Economists said the central bank may have room to trim rates later on this year, but the international interest rate environment is altering, with U.S. rates rising 25 basis points this week, and it will not oil the wheels for Italy to cut.
Chiara Manenti, economist at Italian brokers Caboto, saw dim prospects for a fall in Italy's 6.75 percent discount rate.

"Italian rates and the lira will not be influenced by the approval of the mini-budget. EMU prospects are moving Italy's financial markets, not its economic fundamentals which are already good," she said.
The lira, reinstated in Europe's exchange rate mechanism late last year, is the primary Bank of Italy concern while inflation continues to remain at low levels, analysts said.

The currency, which has an ERM central parity against the mark of 990, has suffered from spreading concern in the last few months that Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) may be delayed from its projected 1999 start.
A delay for EMU as a whole prompts fears that Italy will not continue its recent drive for fiscal discipline.
The lira has been sold back to 1,007 in the last month, still within its 15 percent ERM fluctuation limits but further from the 990 rate than the Bank of Italy is deemed to like.
De Gregorio said the central bank would not act until market confidence in EMU was fully restored, probably by a sign from Germany it was doing all it could to meet EMU criteria on time.
"Only then will the lira regain its fundamental strength and it's only when the lira is in full health that monetary authorities will feel able to ease official rates," he said.
The Bank of Italy last cut its discount rate in January and in total has sliced 225 basis points off its official rates since July last year.

Francesco Giordano, economist at Credit Suisse First Boston in London, doubted rates would fall further for at least three months, with the Bank of Italy watching for tentative signs of growth in Europe, a change in the international rate environment and signs of a structure-oriented reform programme in Italy.
"This outweighs the good inflation news expected next month. I expect the Bank of Italy to wait and see maybe until the second half of the year," he said.
Provisional data for March showed inflation at 2.2 percent year-on-year -- lowest level for around 30 years.
Giuseppe Abbotto, analyst at Banque Indosuez here, said with low inflation data in April and a stronger dollar aiding the lira, the Bank of Italy could allow money market rates to fall.
"But I don't expect official rates to be touched before the second half of May," he said.
